    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--a', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--b', type=str, required=True)

    f = furl(args.a)
    print(f.scheme)

    print(f.path)
    print(f.query.add({args.b: args.c}))
    print(f.url)

All three args are REQUIRED. It prints exactly 5 lines:
  line1 = f.scheme      (Python None prints as "None"; empty string prints as "")
  line2 = f.host
  line3 = f.path
  line4 = str(f.query) AFTER add({b: c})
  line5 = f.url AFTER that mutation

- Use a bash helper so output is unambiguous. Example:
    p(){ echo "IN=[$1] b=[$2] c=[$3]"; /workspace/dataset/test6_executable --a "$1" --b "$2" --c "$3" 2>&1 | cat -A; echo "rc=$?"; }
  cat -A makes trailing spaces / CR / non-ascii visible ($ = end of line, M- sequences = high bytes).
- Use single quotes in bash to avoid shell mangling.
- To distinguish "empty string" from "None" on a line: cat -A shows "$" for empty and "None$" for None.
- Note lines 4 and 5 reflect the MUTATION (the added b=c pair). To see the *original* query you must
  reason by subtracting the appended pair, or use a b/c pair you can recognize (e.g. b=Z c=Z).
- Some inputs may make the program CRASH (traceback) or exit nonzero. Record those exactly:
  the exception type and message matter, but for our port we mainly need to know WHICH inputs crash.
- Run MANY probes (30+). Be systematic: vary one thing at a time. Confirm every rule with at least
  two independent examples, and actively try to FALSIFY each rule you form.

OUTPUT CONTRACT: return findings as structured data. Rules must be precise enough that another engineer
can implement them in JavaScript WITHOUT running the executable. Always attach the literal probe
transcripts (exact argv you passed, exact 5 output lines) that justify each rule.

The port must behave identically for argv handling. Probe the executable's argv behavior and record
EXACT stdout/stderr text and EXIT CODES (use: cmd; echo "rc=$?"  and redirect 2>&1, but also check
which stream each message goes to by testing 2>/dev/null and 1>/dev/null separately).

"--a=value" equals-form; "--a value"; abbreviation and prefix forms; "--" alone; "-a" single-dash;
repeated "--a x --a y" (last wins?); a value that starts with a dash: --a -5 and --a=-5 and --a "--b";
empty value --a ""; a value containing spaces; extra positional args "foo";
order permutations (--c v --a v --b v). Record the EXACT usage/error message text including the program
name shown (note: the program name comes from sys.argv[0] basename — report the literal string used,
e.g. "test6_executable"), the exact wording of errors like
"error: the following arguments are required: --a, --b, --c", and the exact exit codes (2 for errors, 0 for --help).
Also report whether usage goes to stdout or stderr for --help vs for errors, and the exact blank-line
and indentation layout of the --help output.

rules.rule: Program name (`prog`) = POSIX basename of argv[0]. It is used verbatim in the usage line and as the prefix of error lines. When invoked as /workspace/dataset/test6_executable the literal string is `test6_executable`; via a symlink named `myalias` it is `myalias`; via a copy named `renamed.bin` it is `renamed.bin`. No extension stripping.
rules.evidence:
argv: ./myalias --help  -> stdout line1: `usage: myalias [-h] --a A --b B --c C`
argv: /tmp/argvA/renamed.bin (no args) -> stderr: `usage: renamed.bin [-h] --a A --b B --c C` / `renamed.bin: error: the following arguments are required: --a, --b, --c`
argv: ./test6_executable from /workspace/dataset -> `usage: test6_executable [-h] --a A --b B --c C`

rules.rule: The usage string is exactly `usage: {prog} [-h] --a A --b B --c C` (one line, no trailing space) at the default terminal width of 80. Metavars are the uppercased dest: A, B, C.
rules.evidence:
argv: (none)
stderr:
usage: test6_executable [-h] --a A --b B --c C
test6_executable: error: the following arguments are required: --a, --b, --c
rc=2 (od -c confirms no trailing spaces, single \n line endings)

rules.rule: `--help` or `-h` (anywhere in argv, including after other options, and including unique long-prefix abbreviations `--h`, `--he`, `--hel`) prints the help text to STDOUT and exits with code 0. STDERR is empty. Help fires immediately when the token is scanned, so it wins over missing-required-args and over unrecognized-args errors.
rules.evidence:
argv: --help  -> STDOUT:
usage: test6_executable [-h] --a A --b B --c C

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit
  --a A
  --b B
  --c C
STDERR: (empty)  rc=0
Same exact output for: `-h`; `--a x --help`; `--help --a x`; `--h`; `--he`; `-h --z`; `--a x --b k --c v -h`; `--a x -h --b k`

rules.rule: Exact help layout (7 lines, each terminated by \n, no trailing blank line): line1 usage; line2 empty; line3 `options:`; line4 `  -h, --help  show this help message and exit`; line5 `  --a A`; line6 `  --b B`; line7 `  --c C`. Indent is 2 spaces; the help-text column starts at character index 14 (2 spaces indent + 10-char `-h, --help` + 2 spaces). Section header is `options:` (Python >= 3.10 wording), NOT `optional arguments:`.

rules.rule: Missing required options produce `{prog}: error: the following arguments are required: {list}` where {list} is the missing option strings joined by `, ` in DECLARATION order (--a, --b, --c), independent of argv order.
rules.evidence:

argv: --a http://x.com -> `...required: --b, --c`
argv: --b k -> `...required: --a, --c`
argv: --c v -> `...required: --a, --b`

argv: --b k --c v -> `...required: --a`
All rc=2

rules.rule: Leftover/unknown argv items produce `{prog}: error: unrecognized arguments: {extras}` where {extras} are the leftover tokens in ORIGINAL argv order joined by a single space (tokens are NOT quoted/escaped, so an empty or space-containing token is ambiguous in the message). This check runs LAST, after the required-args check.
rules.evidence:
argv: --a x --b k --c v --z -> `unrecognized arguments: --z`

argv: --z (alone) -> `the following arguments are required: --a, --b, --c` (NOT unrecognized) — proves required beats unrecognized
All rc=2

rules.rule: An option that consumes a value but has none left (or whose next token is parsed as an option) produces `{prog}: error: argument --X: expected one argument`. This is raised during the left-to-right scan, so it beats the required-args check and beats a later `-h`.

argv: --a x --b k --c -h -> `argument --c: expected one argument` (help NOT printed, rc=2)
argv: --a x --b k --c --help -> `argument --c: expected one argument`
argv: --a x --b k --c v --b -> `argument --b: expected one argument`

rules.rule: Both `--opt value` and `--opt=value` forms are accepted and equivalent. For the `=` form only the FIRST `=` splits; the remainder (including further `=`) is the value. `--opt=` yields the empty string.

argv: --a=--b=1 --b k --c v -> line3 `--b=1`

rules.rule: Repeating an option: LAST occurrence wins (store action overwrites). Applies to --a, --b, --c, and mixes freely with the `=` form. Order of the three options in argv is irrelevant.

rules.rule: Long-option abbreviation (allow_abbrev default True) is enabled: any unique prefix of a defined long option is accepted. Only `--help` is abbreviable here (`--h`, `--he`, `--hel`); `--a`/`--b`/`--c` are already minimal, and any longer string like `--ab`, `--aa`, `--a--`, `--A` is NOT an abbreviation (matching is by prefix, and is case-sensitive) so it becomes an unrecognized token.

rules.rule: Single-dash `-a`, `-b`, `-c` are NOT defined; they are treated as unknown optionals and land in the leftovers. Single-dash clustering IS applied for the defined short flag `-h`: `-hh` and `-hx` both fire help (the `-h` prefix matches, remainder is re-split into further short options and help exits immediately), while `-xh` does not.
